description: A→B means that an algorithm for B can solve A under the stated construction and assumptions. T is the source runtime on the displayed virtual instance; α is its approximation guarantee in the stated minimization or maximization convention. Exact schedules are shown only when the construction certifies them. Conditional simulations require matching the source graph class, coefficients, costs and initial information. LP relaxation alone gives no integral solution.

entries.title: Neighborhood set cover

instance.description: One variable/set copy and one request/element copy per vertex, with a virtual edge for membership in a closed neighborhood. Self-membership is a local virtual edge.

conditions: Use universe V and the set N[v] for each candidate vertex v, with the candidate’s cost. A chosen set corresponds to choosing its vertex, so integral OPT is unchanged.

Each real vertex hosts its two virtual copies. Precompute both outgoing message sets at a virtual round’s start, then deliver the set-copy and element-copy messages in two physical phases. This gives the displayed 2T schedule, including T=0.
The maximum set size and element frequency are both at most Δ+1. Any source theorem’s initial labels and global parameter knowledge must be supplied or their setup cost added.
Apply graph-class assumptions to the transformed incidence graph. Planarity is not preserved: planar K4 has closed-neighborhood incidence graph K4,4.
The displayed CONGEST simulation is per-edge. Additional broadcast or stronger anonymity conventions must be checked for the particular algorithm.
The transformed closed-neighborhood incidence graph has exactly n+2m edges: n self-incidences and two incidences for every original edge.

entries.title: Edges as universe elements

instance.description: The vertex–edge incidence graph, obtained by subdividing each original edge once. Original-vertex processors have degree at most Δ; edge processors have degree two.

conditions: Use universe E and one set of incident edges for each vertex, with the same vertex cost. Every element has frequency two, and each set has size at most Δ.

A one-round identifier exchange lets endpoints agree on ownership and unique identifiers for virtual edge processors. One incidence round can then be simulated in one physical round, with local messages at the owner delivered locally. If the necessary endpoint identifiers are initially known, the setup can be omitted.
The source theorem’s global instance-size or degree information must also be supplied; obtaining it is not hidden in T+1.
Subdividing edges preserves planarity, but arbitrary incidence-network and minor promises still need checking. A generic per-edge simulation does not preserve a broadcast-only restriction.
Anonymous broadcast algorithms can sometimes avoid identifier-based ownership; such a specialized simulation is not certified by this generic recipe.
The displayed maximum degree max{Δ,2} applies when G has at least one edge. An edgeless instance is handled locally with the empty output; it is not passed to the incidence algorithm.
The edge-subdivision incidence graph has exactly 2m edges, with two incidences for each original edge.

entries.title: Vertex-capacity packing constraints

instance.description: The vertex–edge incidence graph, obtained by subdividing each original edge once. Original-vertex processors have degree at most Δ; edge processors have degree two.

conditions: Use one nonnegative variable per edge, with incident-variable sum at most one at each vertex. The objective is matching cardinality or the supplied edge weights.

Host an edge-variable processor at an endpoint agreed by an identifier exchange; one incidence round then takes one physical round. A final output notification lets both endpoints learn their edge value. Setup and notification give O(T+1); any extra source parameter knowledge must be supplied separately.

For unit edge weights, write the algorithm’s dual as max 1ᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤1, with A the edge-by-vertex 0–1 incidence matrix. Then Γd=2 and Γp≤Δ. The selected packing theorem’s normalization and bit encoding must hold.
Fractional degree constraints do not enforce integral matching on nonbipartite graphs. No rounding or odd-set constraints are included.
The displayed maximum degree max{Δ,2} applies when G has at least one edge. An edgeless instance is handled locally with the empty output; it is not passed to the incidence algorithm.

entries.title: Domination on the line graph

instance.description: There is one virtual vertex per original edge. Two virtual vertices are adjacent exactly when their original edges share an endpoint. Here m=|E(G)| and Δ_L=max over uv∈E(G) of (deg(u)+deg(v)−2); Δ_L≤2Δ−2 when the graph has an edge. Edgeless inputs return the empty set locally.

conditions: A selected vertex of L(G) corresponds to the original edge. Feasibility and cardinality OPT agree; weighted transfer additionally requires an algorithm accepting the corresponding vertex weights.

Assign each virtual edge-node to an endpoint. With unrestricted LOCAL messages, a virtual round routes through shared endpoints in at most two physical rounds; constant setup and output notification give O(T+1).
The source algorithm must accept the line graph’s n′, Δ′, IDs and any supplied parameters. Obtaining global information is not free.
A line graph can be much denser and need not preserve planarity: the line graph of a star is a clique.
This recipe claims LOCAL only. Arbitrary different messages along virtual adjacencies can create congestion at physical edges, so an O(T) CONGEST simulation is not inferred.
Exact algorithm substitutions use n′=m and Δ′=Δ_L, where Δ_L=max_{uv∈E(G)}(deg(u)+deg(v)−2). The displayed 2Δ−2 is an upper bound, not an exact substitution in a nonmonotone theorem.
For simple G, m_L=sum_v binom(deg(v),2) is the exact number of edges of L(G). It is retained symbolically rather than replaced by a monotone upper bound.

entries.title: Threshold at one half

instance.description: The original communication graph and its structural parameters are unchanged.

conditions: The algorithm returns a feasible fractional vertex cover x on the original graph, and each vertex knows its own coordinate. Let D contain exactly the vertices with x_v≥1/2.
Every edge has an endpoint in D because x_u+x_v≥1. For nonnegative vertex costs, cost(D) is at most twice the fractional solution cost, hence at most 2α times integral OPT.
Thresholding is local and needs no extra communication. If the fractional algorithm runs on a separate incidence network, its simulation cost must be added before using this recipe.
This recipe changes the factor from α to 2α and is therefore separate from the unrounded relaxation link; it is not an approximation-preserving automatic import.

entries.title: Reuse a connected dominating set

instance.description: The same connected input graph, restricted to unit vertex costs. All source algorithm inputs remain required.

conditions: On a nonempty connected graph with unit vertex costs, run the source connected-dominating-set algorithm and return exactly its selected vertices as an ordinary dominating set.
OPT_MDS ≤ OPT_CDS ≤ 3 OPT_MDS − 2. Thus an α-approximation against integral OPT_CDS gives a 3α-approximation against integral OPT_MDS, with no additional communication.
The optimum comparison is unweighted. On a three-vertex path with costs (1,M,1), ordinary domination costs at most 2 while every connected dominating set costs at least M.
The target remains restricted to connected inputs. Do not extend a connected-input algorithm to disconnected networks without checking component-wise operation, termination and global inputs.
No fractional-MDS benchmark or lower-bound transfer is inferred by this factor-changing rule.
entries.summary: Reuse a connected dominating set without extra rounds; comparing the unweighted optima costs a factor of at most three.

entries.title: Connect a dominating set locally

instance.description: The same connected input graph, restricted to unit vertex costs. All source algorithm inputs remain required.

parameterDefinitions.description: Maximum |E(H)|/|V(H)| over depth-one shallow minors H of the input graph; needed only for the size analysis

conditions: The input is nonempty, connected and unweighted, and nodes have distinct identifiers. Run the source MDS algorithm on this same graph first.

Three LOCAL rounds reveal radius-three neighborhoods including dominating-set flags. Nearest-dominator clusters, with identifier tie-breaking, have radius one; contracting them produces a connected depth-one minor H with |D| vertices.

For each adjacent cluster pair choose one canonical dominator-to-dominator path of length at most three. In one more round its endpoints notify its at most two internal vertices. Return D and all selected internal vertices.

The checked size count is |D′|≤|D|+2|E(H)|≤(1+2∇₁)|D|. As OPT_f(MDS)≤OPT_MDS≤OPT_CDS, integral or fractional MDS benchmarks can seed an integral-OPT_CDS guarantee; the original benchmark stays in source provenance.

Planar shallow minors have density at most 3, giving multiplier 7. Forest and pseudoforest shallow minors have density at most 1, giving multiplier 3. These bounds also apply through the graph-class inclusion network.

This connector uses unrestricted LOCAL messages. A CONGEST or Anonymous source algorithm can seed it in LOCAL with the necessary identifiers; the derived algorithm is labelled LOCAL. No four-round CONGEST/anonymous connector or lower-bound transfer is inferred.

Clarification pending: preprint Lemma 16 states the stronger size bound 2d|D|. On P9, D={2,5,8} and valid depth-one density bound d=1 give 6, but every connected dominating set has size at least 7. The atlas therefore uses the independently checked 1+2∇₁ count. This example concerns the size lemma and does not itself refute Theorem 17’s approximation ratio.
entries.summary: Connect a dominating set in four extra LOCAL rounds with checked multiplier 1+2∇₁: 7 on planar graphs, 3 on pseudoforests.
